Chapter 5: Sisyphus and the Meaning Found in Daily Struggle
You know, there’s this old story about a man who’s forced to push a huge boulder up a hill—only to watch it roll right back down, every time he gets close to the top.
Day in and day out, he does the same thing. No finish line, no escape, just endless effort.
For most people, this whole story feels like a warning—a symbol of pointless suffering, or maybe even a reminder that life can be, well, kind of futile sometimes.
But what if that’s not the whole picture?
Picture the man, alone on that mountainside. He watches the rock tumble back down, and in that quiet moment—just before he starts again—he finds a sliver of freedom.
He’s accepted his fate. And in that acceptance, there’s a kind of peace. The struggle itself becomes meaningful—not because he’ll ever win, but because it’s his struggle. He owns it.
That’s the heart of the absurd: meaning isn’t handed to you. You create it, right in the middle of living your life.
All those daily struggles, the boring routines, every small win or setback—they can be sources of meaning, if you face them honestly.
Think about a nurse working long hours in a busy hospital. The patients never stop coming, and the demands never really end. It’s overwhelming.
But in the act of caring for someone, in those tiny moments of kindness or connection, there’s purpose. Sure, the work is never finished, and the problems won’t all disappear. But the struggle itself starts to mean something.
So, the story of Sisyphus? It’s not just about despair. It’s actually about defiance.
Even when everything seems meaningless, there’s still a way to live with dignity—and even joy.
The real trick isn’t hoping for some escape or a different fate. It’s about embracing the struggle, and making it your own.
Most of us spend our whole lives searching for meaning, thinking we’ll stumble on it one day. But here’s what the absurd teaches us: meaning isn’t something you find. It’s something you make.
It’s built in the act of living, in the choices you make every day, in refusing to give up—no matter how tough things get.
The routine, the daily grind, those small acts of kindness or courage—these are what give life meaning.
Not because they guarantee happiness or success, but because they’re little acts of rebellion against the absurdity of it all.
In the end, it’s not really about the outcome.
It’s about the struggle itself.
